notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.35_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.35.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.35.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.

---

### Changed

- **The rooms column is a gutter of places and one list.** Every server you
  belong to is an icon down the left edge now, always visible, with the people
  you know at the top of it — so switching between them is a glance and a
  click rather than a scroll. The Servers/Friends tabs are gone; those two
  buttons are what the tabs were.

  What is left of the column is about one place at a time, and it has stopped
  drawing boxes around itself: the card around the open server, the border
  around "Start a live chat", and the block of solid colour on the channel you
  are reading are all gone. A channel is its name, and the one you have open
  is marked the way an unread one is — by weight and colour, not by being the
  loudest thing in the window.

- **A blue accent, and corners with a little more give.** The app was keyed to
  a green; it is keyed to a blue now, and every colour that comes off it — the
  channel you are in, a link, your own messages, the tray icon — follows.
  Corners went from three pixels to four.

- **Android has the same window the desktop does.** The gutter of places is
  down the left edge there too: every server you belong to, and the people you
  know above them, one tap from wherever you are. Tapping a place shows what
  is in it — its channels and whoever is talking in them — and tapping a
  channel gives the conversation the whole screen, with a way back in its
  header. What this replaces is a Servers/Friends bar along the bottom, which
  cost the same sixty pixels and carried two buttons instead of every server:
  reaching another place from a conversation was three taps where it is now
  one.

- **GIF search and Emoji are one section with link previews.** Three separate
  pages of settings that all answered the same question — what this window may
  go and fetch from somewhere other than the people you are talking to — are
  now one, called Content.

### Fixed

- **The camera did not work on Linux at all.** Pressing anything that opened
  it failed with "NotAllowedError", including the preview in settings. The
  webview asks permission before handing over a camera, and asks by a route
  nothing was listening on, so every request was refused with no prompt and no
  way to say yes. Screen sharing was refused the same way.

- **Opening the camera settings could freeze the whole window.** On a Linux
  machine without GStreamer's audio plugins installed, showing a camera took
  the page down with it — the light came on and the app stopped answering.
  The app now checks before it opens anything and says which package is
  missing.

- **Sharing a screen on Linux failed with "Invalid constraint".** The request
  asked for a size and a frame rate as preferences, which nothing is supposed
  to refuse; WebKit refused them anyway. It now asks again without them, and
  scales what arrives down to the size it wanted.

- **The camera picker listed the same camera twice.** Once because the webview
  reports one camera twice on most runs, and once because a single camera was
  named both by the "system default" row and by its own row underneath. The
  second of those happened on every platform.

- **The microphone picker listed things that are not microphones.** Rate
  converters, channel mixers, both sound servers and "Discard all samples"
  came back from the system alongside the actual hardware — fifteen entries in
  front of four real devices. Only devices are offered now.
